chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Wider Lens on Risk

lessons.title: Smoothed Returns: Why Appraised Assets Hide Their True Volatility

children.text: Ask anyone who bought a flat in Noida or Thane around 2014 whether it lost value over the next five years, and most will say no. The price never went down, they will tell you. It just stopped going up. Meanwhile, builders in those markets were quietly offering free parking, stamp duty waivers and "no EMI till possession" schemes, which are price cuts that never appeared on a rate card. The owners were not lying. Their flats had no daily price, so the fall simply never got recorded. That is return smoothing, and it is why so many alternatives look far calmer on paper than they really are.

body.text: A smooth return line does not mean a calm asset. It usually means the asset is measured rarely, by people anchored to the last number, so real swings get spread out, delayed and quietly shrunk.

children.text: Why Appraisals Smooth Returns

markDefs.definition: The tendency of appraisal-based values to move more gradually than true market values, which makes reported returns look less volatile than the asset really is.

children.text: Nobody sets out to hide volatility.
Appraisal smoothing
happens naturally, for three reasons:
Infrequent measurement.
A value checked once a quarter or once every six months cannot show what happened in between. A crash and a recovery inside one period can vanish entirely.
Backward-looking evidence.
Valuers rely on recent comparable deals. In a falling market, few deals happen, and the ones on record were struck at older, higher prices.
Anchoring and reluctance.
It is professionally and commercially uncomfortable to cut a value by 25% in one go. Marks tend to come down in small, gradual steps instead.
Watching Smoothing Happen

A simple way to model an appraisal is to treat each new value as a blend of the true market value today and the previous appraisal. Here α (alpha) is how much weight the valuer gives to today's true value.

body.caption: A = appraised value, V = true market value, t = this quarter, α between 0 and 1

children.text: Take a hypothetical portfolio of office buildings over eight quarters. Its true market value rises, crashes by about a quarter, then recovers. The valuer uses α = 0.4, giving 40% weight to current conditions and 60% to the last appraisal.

body.title: True market value vs appraised value of an office portfolio (index, start = 100, illustrative)

stats.label: Annualised volatility: appraised
stats.context: Less than half the real figure

children.text: Look at three things in the chart. The appraised line falls only half as far. It hits bottom in Q5, a full quarter after the true value had already started recovering. And by Q8 it is only just back to where it started, even though the true value is already 6% higher. Smoothing does not remove losses. It spreads them over more quarters, delays them and shrinks their peak.

body.title: Show me how analysts unsmooth reported returns

markDefs.definition: When one period's return tends to resemble the previous period's return. Strong serial correlation in reported returns is a classic sign of smoothing.

children.text: Smoothed returns show strong
serial correlation

: a bad quarter tends to be followed by another bad quarter as the valuer catches up. Analysts reverse the blending formula to estimate the true return hiding underneath. This is a simplified version of a method widely used in real estate research.

content.caption: Estimates this period's true return from this period's and last period's reported returns

children.text: Example: a fund reports −2% this quarter and −1% last quarter, and you assume α = 0.4. The estimated true return is (−2% − 0.6 × −1%) ÷ 0.4 = (−2% + 0.6%) ÷ 0.4 = −3.5%. The real quarter was well over one and a half times as bad as reported. The hard part in practice is that nobody knows the true α, so treat the result as an estimate.

body.title: Unsmooth a quarter
body.prompt: A real estate fund reports a return of −3% this quarter and −1% last quarter. Assume α = 0.5. Using the unsmoothing formula, what is the estimated true return this quarter, in percent?
body.explanation: (−3% − 0.5 × −1%) ÷ 0.5 = (−3% + 0.5%) ÷ 0.5 = −2.5% ÷ 0.5 = −5%. The fund's reported −3% understates a quarter that was really closer to −5%.

children.text: Two Prices for the Same Buildings

Listed REITs give you a rare live view of smoothing, because each one has two values at once: an appraised NAV based on periodic valuations of its buildings, and a unit price set by buyers and sellers on NSE every day. When markets panic, the gap between them tells you how far the appraisal is lagging behind what investors will actually pay.

body.caption: A hypothetical Indian office REIT before and during a market crash (illustrative)

children.text: The same buildings, the same tenants, the same week. One number says the asset lost 2%. The other says investors would pay 24% less for it. If you owned those buildings directly or through an unlisted fund, you would see only the first number, and you would still face the second one if you tried to sell.

body.text: Part of a listed REIT's price drop in a crash is market panic, not a change in the buildings' long-term worth, so neither number is perfectly "true." But the listed price is what money actually changes hands at. The appraised NAV is an opinion about what it should change hands at.

children.text: Why Smoothing Matters for Your Decisions

markDefs.definition: Return earned above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility taken. Calculated as (return minus risk-free rate) divided by volatility. Higher looks better.

children.text: Smoothing is not just a reporting quirk. It flatters every risk-adjusted measure built on volatility, including the
Sharpe ratio
. Critics sometimes call this "volatility laundering": an asset looks safer simply because it is priced less often.

body.caption: How smoothing flatters the Sharpe ratio (illustrative, risk-free rate 6.5%)

children.text: On reported numbers, the fund looks more than twice as good as the Nifty on a risk-adjusted basis. Unsmoothed, it looks worse. Any comparison, allocation tool or adviser's pie chart that feeds in reported volatility will push you to hold too much of the smoothed asset.

body.title: What smoothing does to your view of a portfolio

columns.label: What the reports show
points: Little connection to stock market crashes
A portfolio that seems to have held up in a sell-off

columns.label: What is really going on
points: Real swings spread over more periods and delayed
Crashes that show up a quarter or two later
An allocation to alternatives that has quietly grown too large

body.text: Beware of exits priced at stale values. If a fractional platform or open-ended fund lets investors buy or sell at the last appraised value during a falling market, those who leave early get paid too much, and the investors who stay absorb the shortfall when values finally catch up.

body.title: Spot the smoothing
body.question: Which pattern in a fund's reported quarterly returns is the strongest sign of appraisal smoothing?
options: Returns that swing sharply between large gains and large losses each quarter
Returns that move in small steps, with losses arriving one or two quarters after listed markets fell
Returns that exactly match the Nifty 50 every quarter
A single very large loss in the same quarter as a stock market crash
body.explanation: Smoothing produces small, gradual moves with strong serial correlation, and losses that lag listed markets. A large loss in the same quarter as a crash suggests the fund is marking to market promptly, which is the opposite of smoothing.

body.title: Name the pattern
body.textWithBlank: When one period's reported return tends to resemble the previous period's, the returns are said to show serial ___.
body.explanation: Serial correlation, also called autocorrelation, is the statistical fingerprint of smoothing. Market-priced assets like the Nifty 50 show very little of it from quarter to quarter.

body.title: Rahul's portfolio after a crash
body.scenario: Rahul, 47, a CA in Jaipur, has a ₹1 crore portfolio with a 60:40 target: ₹60 lakh in equity mutual funds and ₹40 lakh in a real estate AIF. A sharp market crash hits. His equity funds fall 30%. The AIF's next report shows a fall of just 2%. Rahul's adviser says: "Your real estate held up brilliantly. You are only down about 19%, and alternatives are now nearly half your portfolio, so they clearly work."
body.prompt: Work out the reported numbers, then explain what they might be hiding and what Rahul should be careful about.
body.modelAnswer:
Reported numbers:
- Equity: ₹60 lakh × 0.70 = ₹42 lakh.
- AIF: ₹40 lakh × 0.98 = ₹39.2 lakh.
- Total: ₹81.2 lakh, a fall of 18.8%.
- AIF share: ₹39.2 lakh ÷ ₹81.2 lakh ≈ 48%, up from 40%.

What may be hiding underneath:
1. The AIF's −2% is an appraisal. If its true market value had fallen, say, 15%, it would be worth ₹34 lakh. The portfolio would really be about ₹76 lakh, down 24%, with the AIF at about 45%.
2. The AIF's losses may simply arrive over the next one or two reports.
3. "Held up brilliantly" confuses measurement with resilience. No buyer was asked to pay the reported value.

What to be careful about:
- Do not treat the jump to 48% as proof the allocation works. It mostly reflects stale pricing, and he cannot rebalance the AIF anyway because it is locked in.
- Do not add more money to the AIF on the basis of its reported stability.
- If rebalancing, adjust using the liquid assets and assume the AIF's value will come down later.

cards.definition: Appraised values moving more gradually than true market values, which understates volatility and drawdowns.
The weight a valuer gives to current market conditions. Lower α means heavier smoothing.
When returns in one period tend to resemble the previous period's. A telltale sign of smoothed returns.
Reversing the smoothing model to estimate the true, more volatile returns underneath reported ones.
A critic's term for assets appearing less risky simply because they are valued infrequently.
When a listed REIT's unit price is below its appraised NAV per unit, often a sign the appraisal lags the market's current view.

points: Appraised assets look calm because they are valued rarely, using backward-looking deals, by people anchored to the last number.
In the illustration, a true 24.1% fall showed up as only 12.4%, and true volatility of 17.6% was reported as 8.1%.
Smoothing does not remove losses. It delays them, spreads them out and shrinks their peak.
Listed REITs reveal the gap: in a crash, unit prices can fall far more than appraised NAV.
Smoothed volatility inflates Sharpe ratios and pushes investors to hold too much in alternatives.
Before trusting a low-volatility figure, unsmooth it in your head: assume the real swings were two to three times larger and arrived later.
